segments.text: History Repeats Itself
Why Sadhana, Not Belief Alone, Leads to Samadhi
Jai Siyaram, Jai Siyaram

Whatever chanting (jaap) you are able to do, try to move into the second stage of practice. Those whose count has crossed 25 lakh may begin the second stage. Those who have received permission for the third stage may practice the third stage, and those permitted for the fourth stage may practice the fourth. But our ultimate goal, across every stage, is one thing: Samadhi.
Samadhi Is Not Sleep — It Is Complete Awakening

Samadhi does not mean “falling asleep” in the way people often imagine it. Samadhi means becoming fully awakened — aware of every movement around you, aware of who has arrived at the gate outside, able to rise and go wherever you need to, free from any bondage of the physical body. This is the final stage every seeker's practice should reach.

The fourth stage itself has four parts (paaths). As soon as a practitioner completes the fourth part of the fourth stage, a state of samadhi begins to arise. Anyone who reaches any point within the fourth stage earns the title of Sadhak — a true practitioner. Before that point, you are not yet a Sadhak. You are only a Bhakt — a devotee.
The Difference Between a Bhakt and a Sadhak

A Sadhak is one who performs sadhana — disciplined spiritual practice. Sadhana is the vehicle that carries us to samadhi. If you have not reached samadhi through any form of dedicated practice, you are still only a devotee, not yet a practitioner. As a devotee, your task right now is simple: deepen your devotion so that you become capable of true sadhana.

When a person truly becomes a Sadhak, they begin to master spiritual energies — and mastering any energy requires sustained sadhana. As it is said: no one has ever attained anything without sadhana. You may sit here and praise us as much as you like, or criticize us as much as you like — it makes no difference. Until sadhana lives in your body, until japa (chanting) lives in your body, until you cross the fourth stage, no samadhi will ever come to you.

Before samadhi arrives, every element within a person must be awakened. Different seekers here are working on different dimensions — some on higher-dimensional energy, some on divine (dev) energies, some journeying through other realms, some simply working through their own nerves, their own blood. Each is refining their own practice, but the shared first milestone for everyone is the fourth stage.
A Story of Misplaced Priorities

Someone who recently entered a Baglamukhi state after crossing into the fourth stage had, before this, wandered through the entire universe in their spiritual search, visited great pilgrimage sites, and still couldn't understand what was happening within them. They came here saying, “Brother, I haven't had darshan in three years.” During the festival (Mahotsav), that darshan finally happened.
And immediately after, the very next question was: “Now tell me — why isn't my marriage happening? I'm thirty-five, forty-five years old, why am I not getting married?”

This person had done three years of sadhana, prayed sincerely — and once their mind opened to it, once they began crossing the third stage, dormant energies within their body separated and surfaced. That is why, for the last three days, this person has taken on the form of Baglamukhi Mata. Until those energies fully release from the body, samadhi cannot be reached.

This is what is meant by: no one attains anything without sadhana. Within all of us live subtle impurities that conceal the divine element (dev tattva). Through sadhana, we filter and refine ourselves — and from that refinement is born tapasya urja, the energy of penance.
Tapasya Energy Moves Against the Planets

Tapasya urja moves in the opposite direction of planetary influence. If you wish to move against the pull of your grahas (planetary influences), you must awaken this energy of penance — and it is awakened in the body only through the Guru. Through the sadhanas given by the Guru, if you advance on the strength of tapasya, you become capable of reaching samadhi.

No matter how much blessing you receive, if you do not do the sadhana yourself — if you do not chant, do not undertake tapasya, do not perform your rituals, cannot sit in one place, cannot complete your own work — nothing will come to you under any circumstance. Remember this first.
The Company of Saints (Satsang)

The second essential is this: you must hold onto the glory of saints, their inspiration, their stories, their wisdom. If you believe you are somehow inferior, or if you sit here thinking “I am a master of everything, I can bend and break any power, I am this, I am that” — then you forget that, through Hanuman ji Maharaj, there are countless — crores — of saints and sages at work here, each with their own dignity, honor, discipline, and code, each acting according to their own will, under the subtle guidance of the Gurudev who presides over all of them.

When the will of all these saints converges into one collective resolve, miracles begin to happen — and that is precisely where Hanuman ji Maharaj stands. Wherever God stands, everything aligns. Or put another way: wherever the collective will of the people turns, God turns with them. Wherever the community of saints becomes united in purpose, God has no choice but to manifest — this is the divine play (leela) of the Lord.

I do not tell you to go chasing after God directly. You should not. God is the master of leela — playful, elusive (“He Muralidhar Chaliya Mohan”). The more you try to catch Him directly, the further He may lead you, in ways you cannot anticipate. So instead: leave God, and chase your Guru.
Guru vaani, Guru vachan — Guru's word is the voice of God.

As the scriptures say: “Pratham bhakti santan kar sanga” — the first form of devotion is the company of saints. When you enter satsang, when you enter the company of saints, I am bound to manifest there — because that is what the first devotion tells us: where saints gather in unity, I must appear.

So: leave God aside first, and hold onto the company of saints. Saints unite on one thing above all — the name of Ram. No saint will ever say the name of Ram is false. Saints may give you many different mantras, many different paths — but ultimately, every saint tradition arrives at the same single name.

Surdas and Tulsidas lived in the same era, without ever meeting — there was no telephone back then — yet their words converged on the same truth. Guru Nanak, in a completely different region, arrived at the very same truth. Saints across all of India, without contact with one another, speak with one voice.

Wherever saints are found, God is found there too. It is only by the Guru's grace that a true saint is found in your life. As Tulsidas says: “Binu Hari kripa mile nahi santa” — without the Lord's grace, saints are not attained. So the search should not be for God directly — the search should be for saints. And saints, across the world, converge on one thing: the name of Ram. Even Guru Nanak bows before Ram Naam. Every saint bows before it. No matter how accomplished a saint may be, in the end, Ram Naam is truth, and truth alone endures.
The Second and Third Forms of Devotion
The second form of devotion is “mam katha prasanga” — glorifying and recounting the stories and virtues of the Divine, together, in the company of others — not wandering alone.

Naturally, being human, there is always some hurt when effort meets criticism. We work hard to create something, and the moment someone says “I didn't like it,” people rush to apologize, worried they've hurt feelings. But not everyone will feel the same way about anything. Just as one person loves dal and another loves paneer — you cannot force your preference on someone else; it will only backfire. If you feel your own resolve or effort was somehow wrong, the real answer is not self-doubt — it is to hold onto the company of saints more closely, because it is in that company that true strength reveals itself.

The third form of devotion is “Guru pad pankaj sewa” — service at the lotus feet of the Guru. Following the Guru's instructions is considered, in devotion, the highest principle of all. If the Guru says “do not do this,” then it is not to be done — whatever the cost, whatever the consequence. The Guru's physical presence may pass, but his word remains. Guru chale gaye, vachan reh gaye — the Guru may leave this world, but his word endures.

Whoever fully contemplates their Guru, meditates on him, and serves at his feet, receives the Lord's grace without fail — even the divine Leeladhar must come and sit at that devotee's doorstep. But whoever cannot bow to their Guru, cannot honor his commands, will not receive the grace even of the Maha Guru — let alone the Guru himself. And without the Maha Guru's grace, the grace of Bhagwan Ram will never come. If your Guru is Hanuman ji Maharaj and you are a devotee of Ram in the Nath tradition, you must follow your Guru's instruction — whether you find it agreeable or not.
History Repeats Itself

You must chant — you have no choice — because, as we studied in the Chandravanshi series, history repeats itself. This is not a flaw or a fault in the pattern; it is by design. When history repeats again and again, it is not out of habit — it is meant to teach. It repeats so that people can learn from past mistakes, evolve, and move forward — not so the cycle can simply be broken.

Lord Krishna's teaching is that there is, in truth, no such thing as a “mistake.” Whether I sit this way or that way — you will call one right and one wrong, and in your next life you will seek permission to sit the “right” way again. But right and wrong themselves are only definitions of time and place. What is true for me may be false for someone else. White wine may bring luck to me, not to you. Ram is God to me — perhaps not to you. I may eat non-vegetarian food; does that trouble you? What is truly “wrong”? Only violence is unambiguously wrong — everything else depends on context.

In India we're taught: “always keep to the left.” Keep left here, and all is fine. Go to Dubai, and the fine will be steep — there, you must keep right. What's right in one place is wrong in another. So right and wrong are, in truth, a matter of space and time.
The One Thing You Can Control: Time, Place, and the Space Element

The right thing, at the right place and the right time, happens on its own — you don't need to force it. Neither time nor place is within human control. You cannot stop time. You cannot fix your place — the Earth itself never stops moving, spinning at tremendous speed on its axis, constantly shifting its position in space. You cannot lock yourself in one place, no matter how much you wish to.
The right work happens only at the right time and right place — and since neither is in your hands, what exactly is there to worry about?

This is why devotion (bhakti) matters so much — because within bhakti lie dimensions that go beyond time and place. This is the one thing that is different from all the rest of the “written” script of your life. Everything else — this body, this birth, this place, this moment — was already destined. Only one element remains independent: the space element, awakened through bhakti and through the remembrance of God's name. That is why divine incarnations occur — for that very space element.

This is why we say: chanting (japa) is the one thing truly in our hands. Someone may set it to a beat and dance to it, someone may count it on a mala, someone may turn it into a melody, someone may weep while chanting it — it does not matter how. What matters is that for as long as we have time, place, and this human life granted to us, we should keep remembering God's name — because a day will come when we are freed from both time and place. This window is limited.
Closing Message
Chant the name of Hanuman ji Maharaj. Open your inner vision as soon as you can. Focus on yourself, and let go of distractions and idle talk.
Jai Siyaram, Jai Ram.

A Note on Practice Stages A question was raised during the session: can the second-stage chanting also be done while participating in mantra chanting sessions, Shaktipath, or Negativity Removal sessions — in addition to regular sadhana? Yes, it can.

Another question: how does one know they have reached the second stage from the first? When you begin to hear your second mantra internally, and you begin doing the mala of that second mantra, you have arrived. For guidance specific to your own progress, speak with your mentor directly.
Jai Siyaram.
